title: Chest pain and breathlessness while walking the dog in a 70-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 70-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and COPD who is in the ED with 2 hours of central chest pressure and breathlessness. The candidate then interprets his observations, 12-lead ECG, bloods and chest X-ray, recognises an NSTEMI, explains how the types of acute coronary syndrome are told apart, and outlines management and safety netting.
focus: Acute chest pain: a focused cardiovascular history with cluster questions, recognising an NSTEMI on ECG and serial troponin, and telling apart STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital with a cardiac catheter laboratory. Bill Russell, a 70-year-old retired car dealer, has been brought in by his wife with chest pain. He is on a trolley in the acute area. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Bill and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Bill's observations, 12-lead ECG, blood results and chest X-ray report. You will be asked to hand over to the cardiology registrar including your interpretation, give your diagnosis and differentials, outline your management, and answer Bill's question about what happens now, including safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bill Russell, a 70-year-old retired car dealer. You sit upright on the trolley, pale and a little sweaty, with a hand on the middle of your chest. You are short of breath and speak in short phrases, pausing to catch your breath. You are worried but polite. A nurse is with the candidate and does what they ask. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

Opening line: “Hi Doc, I have chest pain. Sorry I can't speak too well, I'm finding it hard to talk as I'm quite out of breath... I think I need help.”

If asked to say more: “I haven't treated my body too well over the years. I'm worried it's catching up with me finally.”

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • Site: right in the middle of your chest.
  • Character: a tight pressure.
  • Radiation: down your left arm and a little up into your jaw.
  • Severity: “It got worse as I kept walking, up to about 5/10, and it has stayed at 5/10 since I sat down.”
  • Onset and context: about 2 hours ago, while you were walking the dog with your wife. It came on over a few minutes, not all at once.
  • Time course: constant since it started.
  • Worse: “I kept walking and the pain and shortness of breath got worse.”
  • Better: nothing. Stopping and sitting down have not made it go away this time.
  • Before: “I've had chest pain in the past, but it usually goes away with time.” If asked more: a few times over the last couple of months, walking the dog up the hill, you got a tightness that went within a few minutes of stopping. You put it down to your lungs and did not see anyone about it.

Associated symptoms

  • Yes: short of breath, much worse than your usual; sweaty; you feel sick (no vomiting); a bit light-headed.
  • No palpitations and no fainting.

Other causes (all no; give only if asked)

  • Aorta: the pain is not tearing or ripping, does not go to your back, did not start at full strength in an instant, and has not moved around.
  • Clots: not worse when you breathe in, no coughing up blood, no calf pain or swelling. No recent hospital stay, operation, time laid up in bed or long trips. No previous clots. No sick contacts.
  • Pericarditis and myocarditis: the pain is not sharp and does not change with sitting forward or lying down. No recent cold, runny nose, fever or aches.
  • Lungs: no fever, no new cough, just your usual bit of white phlegm in the mornings, unchanged. The pain did not start suddenly and sharply on one side.
  • Gut: not burning, no acid taste, not related to meals or lying down. Your reflux feels “nothing like this”, and Nexium keeps it under control.
  • Chest wall: no injury. You cannot point to one spot, and pressing on your chest does not hurt.

Past medical history

  • Type 2 diabetes for 10 years. You need insulin.
  • High blood pressure, diagnosed 6 years ago, for which you take perindopril.
  • High cholesterol. If asked: you are not on anything for it.
  • Reflux (GORD), diagnosed 10 years ago, for which you take Nexium.
  • COPD, diagnosed 5 years ago.
  • Hernia operation 10 years ago, when they put in a surgical mesh.
  • No previous heart problems. Your GP did a routine heart tracing at a check-up a couple of years ago and said it was normal; no other heart tests. No clots in the legs or lungs. No cancer.

Bleeding and medicine safety (only if asked)

  • No bleeding problems, no black stools, no vomiting blood, no stomach ulcers, no stroke, no recent operation or injury.
  • No blood thinners and no aspirin. No tablets for erections (such as Viagra or Cialis).

Medications and allergies

  • Symbicort inhaler twice a day.
  • Insulin once a day.
  • Nexium before meals.
  • Perindopril daily.
  • No over-the-counter medicines, vitamins or supplements.
  • Vaccinations up to date. No known drug allergies.
  • If asked, you weigh about 92 kg.

Family history

  • Mother: died of old age at 90.
  • Father: had a heart attack in his 50s and died at 70. He had diabetes.
  • No brothers or sisters. Your 2 children are well.

Social history

  • Smoking: you do not smoke now. You smoked about 5 cigarettes a day from age 25 until you were diagnosed with COPD at 65.
  • Alcohol: socially. No recreational drugs.
  • Work: retired. You worked as a car dealer in a family business for 30 years.
  • Exercise: you cannot do much exercise or you get puffed.
  • Diet: you try to eat a balanced diet but end up eating a lot of fast food.
  • Home: you live with your wife and your dog. Your wife is your main support and does most of the cooking and cleaning. You do some gardening and look after yourself. Your wife is in the waiting room.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are worried you might be having a heart attack like your dad did. You want to know what is going on and to be helped quickly.

  • About 4 minutes into Part 1, whether or not the candidate has asked, say: “Is it my heart, Doc? Dad had a heart attack.”

The nurse and how Bill changes

  • When asked, the nurse gives the triage observations (09:40): HR 94 regular, BP 148/86, RR 27, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, BGL 11.2 mmol/L. She says she repeated them at 09:55: HR 96 regular, BP 144/84, RR 26, SpO2 92% RA, temperature 36.8 °C, pain 5/10. He is on the cardiac monitor.
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 09:45 and the examiner will give it in Part 2. If asked, the cannula is in and bloods (including a troponin) were sent at 09:45.
  • If the candidate orders oxygen, the nurse asks: “He has COPD. What saturation are you aiming for?” If they give a target of 88 to 92%, the nurse says: “He's 92% on room air, so I'll leave it off and keep watching.” If they order high-flow oxygen without a target, the nurse puts it on and the examiner notes it.
  • If the candidate orders sublingual GTN, the nurse checks the BP and gives it. About 5 minutes later Bill says the pain has eased a little, to 3 or 4/10, but has not gone.
  • If the candidate keeps Bill sitting up, he says that is the easiest way to breathe; if they lie him flat, he becomes more breathless and asks to sit up again.
  • For any other medicine, test or call, the nurse says “Will do.” The examiner notes it for marking in Part 2.

Exam findings

  • General: overweight man sitting upright, pale and a little sweaty, speaking in short phrases. Mild use of accessory muscles. No cyanosis. No xanthelasma.
  • Vital signs: as the 09:55 set.
  • Pulses: radial pulse 96, regular, normal volume. Radial pulses equal, no radio-radial delay. Femoral pulses equal.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 144/84, left arm 140/82.
  • Perfusion: peripheries warm, CRT 2 seconds.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: apex not displaced. Dual heart sounds, no added sounds, no murmurs, no pericardial rub.
  • Chest: trachea central. Hyperexpanded chest with equal, reduced expansion. Resonant to percussion on both sides. Breath sounds vesicular but reduced throughout and equal, with a prolonged expiratory phase. No wheeze, no crackles.
  • Chest wall: not tender; pressing does not reproduce the pain.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no epigastric tenderness, no pulsatile mass. Well-healed right inguinal hernia scar.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling, no pitting oedema.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Bill's identity and gains consent.
Recognises a possible acute coronary syndrome from the start: early in the encounter asks for the observations, continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG (or confirms one has been done).
Keeps Bill sitting upright and keeps questions short because he is breathless.
Uses plain language and empathy: acknowledges his breathlessness and pain, and responds honestly to his worry that it is his heart, like his father's heart attack, without false reassurance.
check.d: Can be earned in Part 1 or when Bill asks again in Part 2.

check.x: History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and character: central, a tight pressure
Onset and context: about 2 hours ago while walking the dog, constant since
Radiation to the left arm and jaw
Severity 5/10, steady since he stopped walking
Worse with continued walking; nothing relieves it, including rest

check.x: Asks about previous episodes: elicits exertional tightness over the last couple of months that settled within minutes of rest and was never assessed.
Asks about associated symptoms of ischaemia: breathlessness, sweating, nausea or vomiting, light-headedness, syncope and palpitations.
Asks cluster questions for the other causes of chest pain:
check.d: Full credit when the dissection kid is asked plus clusters covering at least 4 further diagnoses (PE, pericarditis/myocarditis, pneumonia/COPD exacerbation/pneumothorax, GORD, musculoskeletal).

kids.x: Aortic dissection: tearing pain at full strength from the start, radiation to the back, migrating pain, syncope
Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf pain or swelling, immobility, recent surgery or long travel, previous clots
Pericarditis or myocarditis: sharp pain changed by position, recent viral illness, fever, palpitations
Respiratory: fever, new cough or change in sputum, sudden one-sided pleuritic pain (pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, pneumothorax)
Oesophageal or musculoskeletal: burning, relation to meals, acid taste, comparison with his usual reflux; injury, point tenderness, pain on movement

check.x: Asks about cardiovascular risk factors: diabetes (on insulin), hypertension, high cholesterol, smoking with an estimate of pack-years (about 10) and family history.

Takes the past history: type 2 diabetes for 10 years on insulin, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, GORD, COPD and hernia repair with mesh; rules out known coronary disease, previous DVT or PE, and cancer.

Takes the medication and allergy history: Symbicort twice daily, insulin once daily, Nexium, perindopril; no over-the-counter medicines or supplements; no lipid-lowering medicine; no PDE5 inhibitor; no known drug allergies.

Checks for contraindications to antithrombotic therapy: bleeding problems, black stools or vomiting blood, peptic ulcer (given his GORD), stroke, recent surgery or trauma, and current anticoagulant or antiplatelet use.
Takes a family history: father had a heart attack in his 50s and had diabetes.

Takes a focused social history: alcohol, recreational drugs, occupation, exercise tolerance limited by breathlessness, diet high in fast food, lives with his wife who is his main support, independent with daily activities.
check.d: Credit for any four of these.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he fears a heart attack like his father's and feels his health is “catching up” with him.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: speaking in short phrases, pale and sweaty, accessory muscle use; reviews HR, BP, RR, SpO2, temperature and BGL.
Compares the radial pulses and the BP in both arms (and the femoral pulses) for the asymmetry of aortic dissection.
Cardiovascular examination: perfusion (CRT, peripheral temperature), JVP, heart sounds, murmurs (aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation), pericardial rub and peripheral oedema.

Respiratory examination: trachea, expansion, percussion and auscultation, identifying hyperexpansion with reduced but equal air entry and no crackles or wheeze, and stating that the absence of crackles argues against pulmonary oedema, while a chest X-ray is needed to exclude pneumothorax.
Palpates the chest wall and abdomen (epigastric tenderness, pulsatile mass) and examines the calves for DVT.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 27, 26 then 24 and SpO2 92% on room air are in the yellow zone, calling for a clinical review; HR, BP and temperature are white. Notes that SpO2 92% is within his COPD target of 88 to 92%, and that the pain has eased from 5/10 to 2/10 after treatment by 10:45.
check.d: If no analgesia was ordered in Part 1 and the examiner gave pain as still 5/10 at 10:45, credit noting that the pain is ongoing.

check.x: Interprets the ECG: sinus rhythm 94/min with new horizontal ST depression of 1.5 mm in V4 to V6 and 1 mm in I and aVL compared with the 2023 ECG, and no ST elevation in any lead, so it does not meet STEMI criteria.
check.d: Credit approximate depths (about 1 to 1.5 mm); the essential elements are new horizontal ST depression in the lateral leads compared with 2023 and no ST elevation in any lead, including aVR.

check.x: Interprets the hs-troponin T: 62 then 148 ng/L at 1 hour, above the 99th percentile of 14 with a significant rise, showing acute myocardial injury, which with his symptoms and ECG means myocardial infarction.

Interprets at least two of: normal Hb, platelets and coagulation (safe to start antithrombotics); creatinine 108 with eGFR 62 (relevant to anticoagulant dosing and contrast); glucose 11.8 and HbA1c 8.1% (suboptimal diabetes control); LDL 3.8 untreated.
Interprets the chest X-ray: hyperinflation in keeping with COPD, no pneumothorax, consolidation or pulmonary oedema, and a mediastinum that is not widened.

Gives NSTEMI (non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome) as the most likely diagnosis, justified by central pressure radiating to the arm and jaw with breathlessness, sweating and nausea, his risk factors (age, male, diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, ex-smoker, father's MI), new ST depression and a rising troponin.
Gives at least two differentials (aortic dissection and PE preferred), each with a feature for or against from this patient.
check.d: Also accept pneumothorax, COPD exacerbation with a type 2 MI, or GORD.

check.x: Explains how the types of acute coronary syndrome are told apart by ECG and troponin, and states that Bill has an NSTEMI:
check.d: Scored from the answer to question 2.

kids.x: STEMI: new ST elevation in two contiguous leads (or LBBB/paced rhythm with ischaemic symptoms, or posterior MI), diagnosed on the ECG with symptoms; the troponin will rise but reperfusion does not wait for it
NSTEMI: no ST elevation (may be ST depression, T wave inversion or a normal ECG) with a rise and/or fall in troponin above the 99th percentile
Unstable angina: ischaemic symptoms with no ST elevation and no troponin rise

check.x: Management
Keeps Bill on continuous cardiac monitoring, repeats the ECG with any change in or persistence of pain, and refers to the cardiology registrar for admission under cardiology (CCU).
Gives aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dispersed.
Treats the pain: sublingual GTN if systolic BP above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor, then titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic (or IV GTN) if pain persists.
Does not give routine oxygen: states his target SpO2 is 88 to 92% because of COPD, so none is needed at 92%, titrating oxygen only if he falls below target.
Adds a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg loading preferred) and an anticoagulant (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut 12-hourly, about 90 mg, or unfractionated heparin) as agreed with cardiology.
check.d: Accept clopidogrel or prasugrel when named as cardiology directs. Also credit a candidate who names a P2Y12 inhibitor and states that the timing of loading is decided with cardiology because early angiography is planned.

check.x: Risk-stratifies him as high-risk NSTEACS needing angiography within 24 hours, and within 2 hours if pain is refractory or he becomes unstable.
check.d: Credit a GRACE score mentioned as part of this. Also credit angiography within 2 hours when the candidate states the pain persists despite nitrates and opioid.

check.x: Plans the other medicines: a high-intensity statin, a beta blocker once stable, continuing his insulin (dose adjusted while he is fasted for angiography) with BGL monitoring, continuing his PPI and perindopril.
Safety netting

Answers Bill's question in plain words, without jargon: this is a heart attack caused by a narrowed heart artery, he will stay in hospital under the heart team, and a test of the heart arteries is planned.
check.d: Earned from the reply to Bill's question (question 4).

check.x: Tells Bill to let a nurse know at once if anything changes, and names at least three specific red flags to report straight away (returning or worsening pain, more breathlessness, sweating, faintness, palpitations, bleeding or black stools).
check.d: Earned from the reply to Bill's question (question 4).

part2.lead: Here are Bill's observations, the 12-lead ECG the nurse recorded, his blood results and his chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Say nothing during questions 1 to 3. Question 4 is your question: when the examiner turns to you, ask once: “So is it a heart attack, like Dad had? What happens now?”

You are frightened when you hear it is a heart attack. You settle if the candidate explains clearly, without jargon. If they use words like “NSTEMI” or “angiogram”, ask what that means. If they offer to bring your wife in, you are grateful (this is not scored). Do not ask anything else.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 09:40; the nurse repeated the set at 09:55 before medical review and again at 10:45. On room air throughout.
handover.model:
• Read: at 09:40 RR 27 and SpO2 92% on room air are in the yellow zone; HR 94, BP 148/86, temperature 36.8 °C and alert are white. Pain 5/10, BGL 11.2. At 09:55 RR 26 and SpO2 92% stay yellow, HR 96 and BP 144/84 white, pain unchanged at 5/10. At 10:45, after aspirin and GTN, RR 24 and SpO2 92% remain yellow, HR 88 and BP 136/80 white, and the pain has eased to 2/10.
  • Meaning: ischaemic pain responding to treatment, with breathlessness, haemodynamically stable. With the pain easing and no instability or heart failure, he is high risk rather than very high risk at present. SpO2 92% is within his COPD target of 88 to 92%, so the tachypnoea reflects ischaemia on a poor respiratory reserve rather than a need for oxygen. Hyperglycaemia fits his poorly controlled diabetes and stress.
  • Changes: yellow zone values call for a clinical review by the medical officer (here, now). No routine oxygen; titrate only if SpO2 falls below 88%. Document altered calling criteria for SpO2 (target 88 to 92%) with the senior doctor; otherwise SpO2 below 90% is a red zone call. Continuous monitoring; escalate to a rapid response if he enters the red zone (systolic below 90, SpO2 falling, rising RR or HR) or develops an arrhythmia. Recurrent or persisting pain needs a repeat ECG and moves him to the very-high-risk pathway.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: central chest pain; to acute bay, cardiac monitoring on
ECG 09:45; cannula and bloods 09:45; pain unchanged; doctor informed
Repeat set; medicines as charted from Part 1

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Bill Russell, 70-year-old man, recorded 09:45 in the ED (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV). Central chest pain, ongoing at the time of recording.

  • Rate: 94/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +30°.
  • P waves: normal morphology.
  • PR interval: 170 ms.
  • QRS: 96 ms. No pathological Q waves, no bundle branch block. Normal R wave progression.
  • QTc: 440 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: horizontal ST depression of 1.5 mm in V4, V5 and V6 and 1 mm in I and aVL. No ST elevation in any lead, including aVR and V1 to V3.
  • T waves: upright in the leads with ST depression; normal elsewhere.
  • Comparison: previous ECG on file from 2023 (routine GP health check): sinus rhythm 76/min, no ST depression. The ST depression is new.
handover.model:
• Read: checks the patient details and time (09:45, during pain). Sinus rhythm 94/min, normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc, no Q waves, no bundle branch block. New horizontal ST depression of 1.5 mm in V4 to V6 and 1 mm in I and aVL compared with 2023. No ST elevation anywhere, including aVR.
  • Meaning: new ischaemic ST depression during pain: a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. It does not meet STEMI criteria, and ST depression does not reliably localise the culprit artery. The changes are a high-risk feature.
  • Changes: no STEMI pathway activation, but urgent antithrombotic treatment and cardiology involvement. Repeat the ECG every 15 to 30 minutes while pain persists and with any change, looking for evolving ST elevation.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 09:45 from the IV cannula, about 2 hours after the pain began; repeat hs-troponin at 10:45. Lipids non-fasting.
handover.model:
• Read: hs-troponin T 62 ng/L, rising to 148 ng/L at 1 hour, well above the 99th percentile of 14. Hb 142, platelets 236, INR 1.0 and APTT 31 normal. Potassium 4.6 and magnesium 0.82 normal. Creatinine 108 with eGFR 62 (creatinine clearance about 73 mL/min at 92 kg). Glucose 11.8 and HbA1c 8.1%. LDL 3.8, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.4.
  • Meaning: a rising troponin with ischaemic symptoms and new ST depression is an acute myocardial infarction without ST elevation (NSTEMI), not unstable angina. Nothing in the blood count or coagulation stops antithrombotics. Mild renal impairment matters for contrast; enoxaparin needs no dose reduction at this clearance. His diabetes is suboptimally controlled and his LDL is untreated.
  • Changes: start antithrombotics and a high-intensity statin, monitor BGL on his insulin, check renal function before and after angiography, and recheck lipids on treatment.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect, 10:05.

Clinical details: 70-year-old man with central chest pain and breathlessness. Known COPD. ?Pneumothorax ?pulmonary oedema ?mediastinal widening.

Findings:

  • Lungs: hyperinflated, with 7 anterior ribs visible above the diaphragm and flattened hemidiaphragms. No consolidation, collapse or mass. Normal pulmonary vasculature with no upper lobe diversion, interstitial oedema or Kerley B lines.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax and no pleural effusion. Costophrenic angles sharp.
  • Heart and mediastinum: cardiothoracic ratio within normal limits. Mediastinum not widened, aortic knuckle normal, trachea central.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: hyperinflation in keeping with known COPD. No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality; no pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema or mediastinal widening.
handover.model:
• Read: an adequate PA film showing hyperinflation with flattened hemidiaphragms. Clear lungs, no pneumothorax or effusion, no pulmonary oedema, normal heart size, mediastinum not widened.
  • Meaning: the hyperinflation is his COPD. No pneumothorax (a real risk in COPD), no pneumonia and no pulmonary oedema; a normal mediastinum makes aortic dissection less likely, though it does not exclude it.
  • Changes: nothing here stops antithrombotics. With no pulmonary oedema on CXR, a normal JVP and no crackles, there is no evidence of heart failure. With his pain easing to 2/10 after treatment he is high risk (angiography within 24 hours); he moves to very high risk (within 2 hours) if the pain returns or persists despite treatment or he becomes unstable.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bill Russell, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, which type of ACS is it and how are the types told apart, and what else would you consider?
Outline your management of Bill now, here in the emergency department.
Bill now asks you: “So is it a heart attack, like Dad had? What happens now?” Please answer Bill.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Bill Russell, 70, in the ED.
  • Situation: NSTEMI; pain 5/10 on arrival, now 2/10 after aspirin and GTN (or the score the examiner gave); RR 24 and SpO2 92% on room air (yellow zone, within his COPD target), HR 88, BP 136/80.
  • Background: 2 hours of central pressure to the left arm and jaw, started walking, with breathlessness, sweating and nausea; recent exertional tightness. Insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, hypertension, untreated high cholesterol, COPD, GORD, ex-smoker about 10 pack-years, father MI in his 50s. No bleeding risk, no allergies.
  • Assessment: ECG: new horizontal ST depression 1.5 mm V4 to V6 and 1 mm I and aVL, no ST elevation including aVR. hs-troponin T 62 to 148 (rising): NSTEMI. Hb, platelets and coagulation normal; eGFR 62; HbA1c 8.1%; LDL 3.8. CXR: COPD hyperinflation, no pneumothorax, oedema or widened mediastinum.
  • Recommendation: please review and accept under cardiology; advise on P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant; angiography within 24 hours, sooner if pain returns or persists or he becomes unstable.

NSTEMI: exertional central pressure to the arm and jaw with breathlessness, sweating and nausea; recent exertional angina; multiple risk factors; new ST depression; rising troponin.

Types of ACS (ECG and troponin): STEMI: new ST elevation in two contiguous leads (or LBBB/paced rhythm with ischaemic symptoms, or posterior MI). NSTEMI: no ST elevation, troponin rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile. Unstable angina: no ST elevation, no troponin rise. Bill: NSTEMI.

Differentials: at least two, each with a feature for or against; aortic dissection and PE preferred.

  • Aortic dissection: for: hypertension, age. Against: gradual pressure, no tearing or back pain, equal arm BPs, normal mediastinum.
  • Pulmonary embolism: for: breathlessness, SpO2 92%. Against: no pleuritic pain, calf signs or risk factors.
  • Also accept: pneumothorax, COPD exacerbation with type 2 MI, GORD.

1. Monitoring, IV access, repeat ECG with pain, cardiology registrar now, admit CCU. (Escalation triggers are not required for the mark.)
  2. Aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed.
  3. GTN SL if SBP >90 and no PDE5 inhibitor; IV opioid + antiemetic if persists.
  4. No routine oxygen: COPD target 88 to 92%; he is 92%.
  5. P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg load, or named with loading timing left to cardiology) and anticoagulant (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg, about 90 mg, subcut 12-hourly, or UFH) as cardiology agrees.
  6. High-risk NSTEACS: angiography within 24 h; within 2 h if refractory pain or unstable.
  7. Other medicines (any one): high-intensity statin; beta blocker once stable; continue insulin (dose adjusted while fasted for angiography) with BGL monitoring; continue PPI and perindopril.

• Plain words, no jargon (explains any term Bill asks about); acknowledges his fear about his father.
  • Yes, this is a heart attack, caused by a narrowed heart artery.
  • What happens now: he stays in hospital under the heart team; a test of the heart arteries (an X-ray dye test) is planned to find and treat the narrowing.
  • Tell the nurse at once about at least three of: returning or worse pain, more breathlessness, sweating, faintness, palpitations, bleeding or black stools.

ddx.for: Two hours of central pressure to the left arm and jaw on exertion with breathlessness, sweating and nausea, multiple risk factors, new ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL and hs-troponin T rising from 62 to 148 ng/L.
ddx.against: His breathlessness is partly explained by his COPD, but that does not account for the ECG or troponin.

ddx.for: He is 70 with hypertension and has ongoing central chest pain.
ddx.against: The pain built over minutes as a pressure, is not tearing and does not go to the back, the arm BPs are equal and the mediastinum is not widened.

ddx.for: He is breathless with SpO2 92% and RR 27, and at 70 PERC cannot be used.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, immobility, surgery, travel or previous clot, and the ECG and troponin pattern fit coronary ischaemia.

ddx.for: He has COPD and is breathless.
ddx.against: The pain was not sudden or one-sided, breath sounds and percussion are equal, and the chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax.

ddx.dx: Infective exacerbation of COPD with a type 2 myocardial infarction
ddx.for: He has COPD, tachypnoea and SpO2 92% with a raised troponin.
ddx.against: No fever, new cough, sputum change or wheeze, no clear supply and demand trigger (HR 94, SpO2 within his target, normal Hb), and the pain is classically ischaemic.

ddx.for: He has 10 years of GORD on Nexium.
ddx.against: The pain is a pressure brought on by walking, unlike his usual reflux, with arm and jaw radiation, ST depression and a rising troponin.

guide:
In Part 1, Bill answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the triage (09:40) and repeat (09:55) observations when asked. If the candidate asks for the ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 09:45 and will be given in Part 2; this is an artefact of the format, as in practice it is read within 10 minutes of arrival. About 4 minutes in, Bill asks whether it is his heart, so item 5 can be earned in Part 1. Medicines and calls ordered in Part 1 (aspirin, GTN, the cardiology registrar) are noted and credited against the Management items in Part 2. A candidate who orders high-flow oxygen without a target in Part 1 and does not correct it in Part 2 does not get item 37.

History marking: full credit for item 10 needs the dissection kid (critical) plus clusters covering at least 4 further diagnoses (PE, pericarditis/myocarditis, pneumonia/COPD exacerbation/pneumothorax, GORD, musculoskeletal). Bill's earlier exertional tightness (item 8) comes out only if the candidate asks what he means by “chest pain in the past”.

In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order, allowing about 75 seconds each. Before Part 2 the examiner tells the candidate which medicines were given, using only what the candidate ordered in Part 1. If neither GTN nor an opioid was ordered, replace the 10:45 row with RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air, BP 144/84, HR 96, pain 5, distress moderate. If aspirin was not ordered, it has not been given, and item 35 is earned only if the candidate orders it in Part 2. If no analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate pain is still 5/10 at 10:45. Question 4 is asked by the person playing Bill, once: “So is it a heart attack, like Dad had? What happens now?” Items 42 and 43 are earned from the reply. Credit the diagnosis justification from the ISBAR or question 2. Item 32 comes from question 2. Accept ticagrelor, prasugrel or clopidogrel as cardiology directs, and enoxaparin or unfractionated heparin. For item 39, also credit angiography within 2 hours when the candidate states the pain persists despite nitrates and opioid.

A high-performing candidate asks for monitoring and an ECG in the first minute, characterises the pain and its associated symptoms, screens efficiently for dissection, PE, pericarditis, respiratory and oesophageal causes, checks bleeding risk and compares the arm BPs. In Part 2 they identify new ST depression without ST elevation and a rising troponin as an NSTEMI, clearly separate STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina, give aspirin, GTN and antithrombotics, avoid routine oxygen in COPD, risk-stratify to angiography within 24 hours (within 2 hours if refractory), and answer Bill in plain words with clear red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a long unfocused history, omits dissection or bleeding risk, calls the ECG “non-specific”, activates the STEMI pathway for ST depression or waits for more troponins before treating, gives high-flow oxygen to a COPD patient at 92%, or cannot say how the troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina.
explain:
Diagnosis: NSTEMI

Bill has 2 hours of central, tight chest pressure radiating to the left arm and jaw, brought on by walking and not relieved by rest, with breathlessness, sweating, nausea and light-headedness. He has had exertional tightness over recent months that settled with rest, a pattern of stable angina that has now become an acute coronary syndrome. His risk factors are age over 60, male sex, insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, hypertension, untreated hypercholesterolaemia, an ex-smoking history of about 10 pack-years and a father with a heart attack in his 50s. The ECG shows new ischaemic ST depression without ST elevation, and the hs-troponin rises from 62 to 148 ng/L. This is a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

Telling the types of ACS apart

All three types present with ischaemic symptoms; the ECG and troponin separate them.

TypeECGTroponin
STEMINew ST elevation in two contiguous leads, or LBBB/paced rhythm with ischaemic symptoms, or posterior MI; diagnosed on the ECG with symptomsWill rise, but reperfusion does not wait for it
NSTEMINo ST elevation: ST depression, T wave inversion or normalRise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile
Unstable anginaNo ST elevation: ST depression, T wave inversion or normalNot raised

A raised troponin means myocardial injury, not necessarily ACS. Under the Fourth Universal Definition of MI, myocardial infarction needs a rise and/or fall in troponin with clinical evidence of ischaemia. A type 2 MI is a supply–demand mismatch (for example from hypoxia, tachyarrhythmia or anaemia), and troponin also rises in PE, myocarditis, sepsis and kidney disease.

The focused history

Characterise the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, time course, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity), then ask cluster questions for the other causes:

  • Cardiac: ACS (radiation to jaw, arm or epigastrium, sweating, nausea, breathlessness); stable angina (relief with rest or GTN); aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back, migrating pain, syncope); pericarditis (sharp, pleuritic, eased by sitting forward, recent viral illness); myocarditis (palpitations, fever, fatigue).
  • Respiratory: PE (pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, surgery, immobility, travel); pneumonia (fever, cough); pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic pain, COPD or asthma); pleurisy.
  • GI: GORD (burning, meal-related, worse lying, acid taste).
  • Musculoskeletal: sharp pain reproduced by movement or pressure; costochondritis.

Then take the cardiovascular risk factors and, before any antithrombotic, check bleeding, peptic ulcer, stroke, recent surgery and anticoagulant use. Before nitrates, ask about PDE5 inhibitors.

Interpreting the results

RR 24 to 27 and SpO2 92% on room air are yellow zone values on the NSW adult chart and call for a clinical review. By 10:45, after aspirin and GTN, his pain has eased from 5/10 to 2/10 and he remains haemodynamically stable. The ECG shows new horizontal ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL, with no ST elevation: dynamic ischaemic changes, a high-risk feature, but not STEMI criteria. The rising troponin confirms infarction. Normal Hb, platelets and coagulation make antithrombotics safe; the eGFR of 62 matters for contrast; the HbA1c of 8.1% and LDL of 3.8 point to risk factors that need treatment. The chest X-ray shows COPD hyperinflation without pneumothorax, oedema or a widened mediastinum. In a hyperinflated COPD chest, breath sounds cannot reliably exclude a pneumothorax, so the X-ray is needed.

Differentials that matter

Aortic dissection must be considered before antithrombotics: his pain built gradually, is not tearing, does not go to the back, and his arm BPs and mediastinum are normal. PE is unlikely with no risk factors and an ischaemic ECG and troponin pattern; PERC cannot be applied at his age. Pneumothorax is a real risk in COPD and is excluded on X-ray. A COPD exacerbation causing a type 2 MI is unlikely without infective symptoms or a clear supply–demand trigger. GORD does not explain exertional pain, the ECG or the troponin.

Management (Australian ACS guideline 2016, eTG)

  • A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact, continuous ECG monitoring, IV access, and early senior and cardiology involvement.
  • Escalation triggers: repeat the ECG and get a senior review for recurrent or worsening pain; call a rapid response for systolic BP below 90, an arrhythmia or SpO2 below his target.
  • Oxygen is not given routinely when SpO2 is 93% or more. In COPD the target is 88 to 92% (TSANZ), so Bill at 92% needs none.
  • Aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed, unless truly contraindicated.
  • GTN sublingually for ongoing pain (400 microgram spray, repeated every 5 minutes up to 3 doses) if systolic BP is above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor has been taken; IV GTN or titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic for persisting pain. Use the smallest effective opioid dose (e.g. fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV titrated); morphine delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors.
  • P2Y12 inhibitor: ticagrelor (180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily) is preferred in intermediate to high-risk NSTEACS; prasugrel once the anatomy is known and PCI is planned; clopidogrel if these are not suitable. Where early angiography is planned, many centres agree the timing of loading with cardiology.
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut 12-hourly (dose reduced if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min) or unfractionated heparin.
  • Risk stratification and timing of angiography: a validated score such as GRACE helps. Very high risk (ongoing or recurrent pain refractory to treatment, haemodynamic instability, heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complications) needs angiography within 2 hours. High risk (rising troponin, dynamic ST or T changes, GRACE above 140) needs angiography within 24 hours. Diabetes is an intermediate-risk feature that adds to his risk but does not by itself make him high risk. With his pain easing to 2/10 after treatment, Bill is high risk now and moves to very high risk if the pain returns or persists despite nitrates and opioid, or he becomes unstable.
  • Start a high-intensity statin, give a beta blocker within 24 hours if there is no heart failure, bradycardia or shock (a cardioselective beta blocker is acceptable in COPD), continue the ACE inhibitor, continue his insulin (dose adjusted while he is fasted for angiography) with BGL monitoring, avoiding hypoglycaemia, and keep his PPI, which also protects the stomach on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Safety netting and follow-up

While in hospital, Bill should tell a nurse straight away about returning or worsening pain, more breathlessness, sweating, faintness, palpitations or bleeding. Staff repeat the ECG with any pain and call a rapid response for red zone observations or an arrhythmia. Before discharge he needs secondary prevention (aspirin long term, a P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months, a high-intensity statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta blocker as indicated), a GTN action plan (stop and rest, use GTN, call 000 if the pain is severe, worsening or lasts 10 minutes), referral to cardiac rehabilitation, and GP follow-up of his diabetes control and lipids, as set out in the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard.
points: Central pressure radiating to the arm and jaw, brought on by exertion and not relieved by rest, with breathlessness, sweating and nausea in a man with many risk factors is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise; get an ECG within 10 minutes.

STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina are separated by the ECG and troponin: ST elevation means STEMI; no ST elevation with a rise and/or fall in troponin above the 99th percentile means NSTEMI; no ST elevation and no troponin rise means unstable angina.
Before antithrombotics, screen for aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back, unequal arm BPs, widened mediastinum) and for bleeding risk.
In NSTEMI give aspirin 300 mg, GTN if systolic BP is above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor, a P2Y12 inhibitor and an anticoagulant, and avoid routine oxygen; in COPD the SpO2 target is 88 to 92%.

High-risk NSTEACS (rising troponin, dynamic ST changes) needs angiography within 24 hours; refractory pain, haemodynamic instability, acute heart failure or a life-threatening arrhythmia needs it within 2 hours.
Secondary prevention includes dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months, a high-intensity statin, an ACE inhibitor, a beta blocker as indicated, a GTN action plan and cardiac rehabilitation.
